catalog_quote: 4.2. PHONOLOGICAL WORDHOOD. With regard to stress, the prefixes are part of the same word as the stem and the suffixes: Chintang words contain one main stress, and it regularly falls onto the last syllable of the lexical stem (and the first stem in compounds). Prefixes are never stressed, since they are not stems. There is evidence, however, that the prefixes form phonological subconstituents on their own within the word. In the following representation of this, ω2 denotes a level between the phonological word and the phonological phrase, and is the domain for stress assignment; ω denotes a subdomain of ω2, and Σ1 denotes the first part of a bipartite stem. (22) (ω2 (ω pf/Σ1) (ω Σ(′)-sf)) ... [§4.3, p. 58, after ex. (31)] Both ω-domains are, however, part of a single ω2-domain for stress assignment and enclitic hosting.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One main stress per word; it falls on the last syllable of the lexical stem (in compounds, on the first stem). Prefixes are never stressed, and the suffixes that follow the stem are not stressed either, so the position is fixed relative to the stem edge, not to the word edge. The stress domain (ω2) is the whole grammatical word: prefixes + stem + suffixes, and it also hosts enclitics.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds: stress goes to the first stem. Separately, in the Mundum ritual language, binomial 'limbs' each take stress on their first syllable (Vorberg et al. 2009, p. 5, citing Rai 2007) — a register-specific pattern, not a statement about everyday word stress. Dirksmeyer 2008 notes demonstratives huŋ/ba can carry their own primary stress under contrastive use.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the domain of stress assignment is the phonological word ω2 = prefixes + stem(s) + suffixes (the grammatical word), also the host domain for enclitics. The source is a morphology paper on prefix ordering (Language), not a phonology description; the stress statement is a brief one-sentence characterization with no stress-marked examples, although its main claims are corroborated second-hand by Schiering & van der Hulst 2010: 586-587 ('one primary accent which regularly falls on the last syllable of the lexical stem').
new_statements.identity_note: Chintang proper (chhi1245), the variety of Chhintang VDC, Dhankuta District, documented by the Chintang and Puma Documentation Project / Chintang Language Research Program (Bickel, Stoll, Gaenszle, N. K. Rai). The 2007 paper does not name a sub-dialect; Dirksmeyer 2008 mentions two village dialects (Mulgaũ vs. Sambugaũ) differing in minor forms. Not to be confused with Bantawa (bant1281), of which Chintang was once treated as a dialect.

new_statements.quote: There are no pitch or tone contrasts in Chintang. Chintang words contain one main stress, which regularly falls on the last syllable of the lexical stem. With respect to compound forms (for example, compound verbs), the stress falls on the first stem. Prefixes are never stressed because they are part of the same stress word as the stem and the suffixes (Bickel et al. 2007). [...] In short, word stress in Chintang is weak and not distinctive. The only exceptions are certain sequences of words. For example, if we analyze the morphology of some combinations, we find some minimal pairs like: 'khaca 'food dregs', kha'ca 'he will eat us.'

With respect to compound forms (for example, compound verbs), the stress falls on the first stem. Prefixes are never stressed because they…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Bickel et al. 2007 statement (stem-final syllable, first stem in compounds, prefixes never stressed), which Paudyal cites explicitly; it adds that there are no pitch or tone contrasts, that stress is weak and non-distinctive, the two stem/prefix minimal pairs, and that examples are from the Mulgāũ dialect. The catalog record for Chintang currently has an empty rule field; this source supports filling it as stem-final (morphologically determined) stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No tone or pitch contrasts. One main stress per word, on the last syllable of the lexical stem (so suffixes and prefixes are unstressed; prefixes count as part of the stress word but are never stressed); in compounds the first stem carries the stress. Stress is phonetically weak and not lexically distinctive, but because it tracks the stem it can distinguish a bare stem from a prefixed form ('khaca 'food dregs' vs kha-'ca 'he will eat us'; 'maila 'second son' vs ma-'ila 'he will return to us'). The domain of stress assignment is the recursive prosodic word ω2 = (ω prefix/Σ1)(ω Σ(´)-suffixes), following Bickel et al. 2007.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. The representation (2.41) marks only one stress (´) on the stem; nothing on secondary stress or feet.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is 'weak and not distinctive'; apparent minimal pairs arise only where a prefix is present ('khaca vs kha'ca, 'maila vs ma'ila), i.e. morphology shifts the stressed syllable rather than the rule having lexical exceptions. §2.2 (p. 20) adds that vowel length varies 'mainly as a result of syllable stress'. Chapter 12 notes that non-cliticized particles and sometimes =na and hei carry their own stress (pp. 259, 264, ~282).
new_statements.identity_note: Paudyal 2015 (p. 3, p. 7) names ISO 639-3 ctn, the Chintang VDC of Dhankuta district, and two dialects, Mulgāũ and Sambugāũ; unless noted his examples are from the Mulgāũ dialect, and he says the dialects differ only in parts of morphology and lexicon, so the stress statement is meant for the language as a whole. Schikowski 2013 (p. 21) describes the same language (Chintang VDC and neighbouring Āhāle VDC, 4000-5000 speakers). Bickel & Zúñiga 2017 is a typological chapter on polysynthetic languages generally; whether it discusses Chintang stress could not be checked.

new_statements.quote: Turning to phonological cohesion, we again observe that different rules and constraints target partly different domains: Independent stress [pf-V-V2-sf-cl-pa-(fpa)] vs. [fpa]. Evidence: This unit has a single main stress on the V stem (or occasionally on the V2 stem), followed by an optional dactylic pattern of secondary stress in the sf and pa string. Some but not all free phrasal affixes can be stressed on their own. Examples are ki ‘and’ in (16) or naŋ ‘but’ in (17b). (The possibility of stress is what guides orthographic word breaks in our transcripts.)
new_statements.citation: Bickel, Balthasar & Fernando Zúñiga. 2017. The 'word' in polysynthetic languages: phonological and syntactic challenges. In Fortescue, Mithun & Evans (eds.), The Oxford handbook of polysynthesis, 158-185. Oxford: OUP.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (Bickel et al. 2007: one main stress on the lexical stem, prefixes never stressed, first stem in compounds = 'V stem (or occasionally on the V2 stem)' here). Adds: (i) the exact stress domain [pf-V-V2-sf-cl-pa-(fpa)] including clitics and phrasal affixes, versus free phrasal affixes as separate domains; (ii) secondary stress: an optional dactylic pattern through the suffix/phrasal-affix string (the 2007 paper, fn. 7, left the metrical system unanalysed); (iii) main stress can occasionally sit on the V2 stem. Consistent with Paudyal 2015 ('weak and not distinctive', stem-final). No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Chintang the stress word is the string prefix(es)-V stem-V2 stem-suffixes-clitics-phrasal affixes (optionally plus a free phrasal affix); it carries a single main stress on the verb (lexical) stem, occasionally on the V2 stem instead; prefixes are inside the domain but never bear the main stress; free phrasal affixes such as ki 'and', naŋ 'but', kina 'SEQ' can form their own stress domain. Placement is fixed by morphological structure (the stem), not by counting syllables from a word edge or by weight.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'an optional dactylic pattern of secondary stress in the sf and pa string', i.e. optional secondary stresses at dactylic (every third syllable) intervals through the suffix and phrasal-affix string after the stressed stem (p. 22). No weight condition stated for Chintang (the weight-sensitive statement on p. 14 concerns Mapudungun, not Chintang).
new_statements.exceptions: Main stress 'occasionally on the V2 stem' rather than the V stem; 'Some but not all free phrasal affixes can be stressed on their own' (ki 'and', naŋ 'but'; kina SEQ in ex. 26); V2 stems 'start their own domains' for some constraints (Table 4, p. 25). No lexical exceptions to stem stress are listed.
new_statements.identity_note: The work's §3.2 treats Chintang, 'a member of the Kiranti group of Sino-Tibetan.. Eastern branch' (preprint p. 17), with corpus examples tagged CLLDCh.. (Chintang Language Research Program / child-language corpus) and Story.chintang; no dialect (Mulgāũ/Sambugāũ) is singled out. §3.1 treats Mapudungun (Chile/Argentina), which is not this item's language.
